theme.title: OLD SORROW
theme.logline: It has rained on the city of Old Sorrow for ninety-one years. The gutters run to the Sump, and in the Sump the finest ladies and gentlemen of the city beat one another to death for charity.
theme.world: Old Sorrow is a fantasy city of gaslight, soot and brass, built in tiers down the sides of a flooded valley. The rich live up in the Heights under glass umbrellas the size of cathedrals. The poor live in the Drench, where the rain collects. Steam drives everything. Limbs are bought, sold, pawned and grafted at the Limb Exchange on Crutch Street, and an apothecary will sell you a tincture that brings out the person you would be without your manners. At the bottom of it all is the Sump: a drowned amphitheatre where the city's storm drains meet, where the Benevolent Society for the Elevation of the Lower Orders by Pugilism holds its bouts. Everyone fights in their best clothes.

tone.summary: Dignified and extremely violent. Every fighter is a lady or a gentleman, and every fighter is a murderer. The comedy is the distance between the two: the bow before the disembowelling, the apology during it, the condolence card after.
pillars: Manners first. Nobody swears, shouts or sneers. They beg your pardon, they ask permission, they thank you for the bout. The violence is never acknowledged as impolite.
The other self. Every fighter has a tincture that lets out who they would be without their manners. The good self and the bad self are the same person in the same coat.

Dickensian brutality. The workhouse, the debtors' prison, the factory floor, the undertaker's parlour and the pawnshop are where these people come from. The poor are honest about the violence, and the rich have it in writing.

Appeal to the Gallery. The crowd is the fighters' patron, judge and armoury. A fighter who lands something grand turns, bows and appeals to the Gallery's sense of dignity, and the Gallery answers with a weapon or a limb.
Rain on everything. Every surface is wet, every blow throws spray, blood thins to pink in the puddles and runs to the drains.
tone.voice: Lines are short, formal and dry. No modern slang, no profanity, no winking at the camera. Threats are phrased as courtesies ('Might I trouble you for your teeth?'). The horror is in plain description, never in adjectives.
tone.rating: R18+. Blood sprays in arterial arcs, limbs come off, bones come through skin, faces cave in. It is fantasy and it does not have to make sense.
tone.references: Victorian penny dreadfuls, the music hall, the gentleman's duel, the workhouse novel, the doctor who drinks his own draught, gaslit steampunk. Inspiration only: no names, characters, places or likenesses from any existing work are to be used.

gallery.name: the Gallery
gallery.look: Tiers of private boxes round the Sump under dripping cast-iron arches. Ladies and gentlemen in evening dress, top hats and bonnets, umbrellas up, opera glasses, champagne in the rain. The cheap seats at the waterline are dockers, sweeps and clerks in their Sunday best.
gallery.sound: Polite applause that swells into a roar; gasps; 'Hear, hear!'; 'Shame!'; a brass band in a box that plays a fanfare for a knockdown; the rain on a thousand umbrellas.

favour.name: FAVOUR
favour.note: The Gallery's favour is the meter the game calls fury: the same numbers (FURY in src/sim/moves.ts), only the name changes. A fighter earns it by landing blows, taking them, deflecting and throwing; a special costs half of it, a Special Art half, the Tincture all of it.

appeal.name: The Appeal
appeal.input: L2 (taunt), within 120 frames of landing a knockdown, a launcher, a throw, an air grab or a special
appeal.rule: The fighter turns from their opponent, removes their hat or curtseys, and appeals to the dignity of the Gallery. If the blow before it was a good one, the Gallery answers: on the last frame of the taunt, a gift is thrown from the boxes and lands in the Sump within 3 m of the fighter, for anyone to pick up (L1). The gift is picked from the throws below by the fighter's FAVOUR and their weapon affinity: the more favour, the finer the gift. A taunt with no good blow behind it is an impertinence: the Gallery throws rotten fruit and a jeer, and the fighter loses 10 FAVOUR.
appeal.note: The taunt and the fury it fills are in the game today (TAUNT in src/sim/moves.ts); the gift is not. Thrown limbs can reuse the reattach system that torn-off limbs already use (REATTACH).

tincture.name: The Tincture
tincture.note: Each fighter's Status Art. They drink their own draught and their other self comes out for a time: the same person, the same clothes, no manners left. The other self has its own voice lines, its own glow and its own changes to the numbers. Costs all the FAVOUR. When it wears off they are winded for a moment and apologise.

rules: Every hit that lands bleeds. A jab leaves a spray of droplets; a finisher throws an arc; a special or a throw opens an artery that pumps in time with the heartbeat for a few seconds.
Blood mixes with the rain: it hits hard and red, then thins to pink in the puddles and runs to the nearest drain grate. The Sump floor gets redder through the match and the drains glug.

Every craft bleeds its own fluid with the blood: brass weeps clock oil, steel sprays scalding hydraulic water, lead gushes rainwater, porcelain sheds shards, oak spits splinters and tar, glass leaks burning gas, bamboo sprays boiling tea, iron drops glowing coals, whalebone springs its stays, silver never bleeds at all, the bear graft bleeds more than anything, and the pawned limbs bleed whatever they were made of.
Blood clings to clothes and skin and stays for the whole match. White gloves, cuffs and collars are the fighters' tell.
A KO is never just a fall: something comes off, opens or caves in, chosen by the finishing move and the winner's craft.

stages.note: The game's five stages are still dressed for the old theme (src/sim/stages.ts). They keep their ids and their play; this is what each becomes.

redress.name: The Sump
redress.idea: The drowned amphitheatre where the storm drains meet. Ankle-deep water, drain grates that roar when the rain gets heavy, the Gallery in tiers above. The geysers become the drain grates blowing back: a column of black water and whatever was in it.

redress.name: The New Gasworks
redress.idea: A gasometer half built: girders, steam cranes, lit gas jets, a wet plank floor over a long drop.

redress.name: The Clock of Saint Sorrow
redress.idea: The great clock tower in the Heights, its face broken, the pendulum swinging through the floor, the bells ringing on every KO.

redress.name: The Airship Benevolence
redress.idea: The Society's charity airship over the city, on fire: the promenade deck tilting, rain blowing in, gentlemen leaping with umbrellas.

redress.name: The Marshalsea Riot
redress.idea: The debtors' prison yard during a riot: torches, mud, the walls being stormed by creditors.

crafts.name: Clockwork Brass
crafts.look: Polished brass casings over a watch movement, with little glass windows over the escapement and a winding arbour at each joint. Riveted seams, engraved scrollwork, a maker's mark.
crafts.hit: A hard brass knock with a short bright ring on top and a tiny ratchet click after it.
crafts.breaks: The casing dents, then bursts: springs, gear teeth and jewels scatter, and the mainspring whips loose.
crafts.bleeds: Where brass meets flesh, blood and black clock oil weep together.

cue.note: a clockwork brass fist landing on flesh
cue.prompt: A clockwork brass fist lands hard on flesh: a solid metallic knock with a short bright ring on top and a tiny ratchet click after it. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Hydraulic Steel
crafts.look: Blued steel rams in a polished sleeve, red rubber hoses, a brass pressure gauge at the wrist with a needle that swings on every punch.
crafts.hit: A pneumatic hiss as the ram fires, then a short heavy steel slam.
crafts.breaks: The hoses burst and spray scalding hydraulic water; the ram jams out at full stroke.
crafts.bleeds: Steam and scalding water with the blood, which hisses on the wet floor.

cue.note: a hydraulic steel ram punching into a body
cue.prompt: A hydraulic steel ram punches into a body: a sharp pneumatic hiss, then a short heavy steel slam into flesh. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Drainpipe Lead
crafts.look: Dull grey cast-lead drainpipe in soldered sections, a rain hopper at the shoulder, an elbow joint from a gutter; full of rainwater that sloshes and dribbles from the seams.
crafts.hit: A heavy dull thud with water sloshing inside a metal pipe.
crafts.breaks: The pipe splits along a seam and gushes rainwater.
crafts.bleeds: Rainwater pours out with the blood, so the wound washes itself pink.

cue.note: a water-filled lead pipe arm swinging into a body
cue.prompt: A heavy lead pipe full of water swings into a body: a dull heavy thud with water sloshing inside the metal. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Kiln Porcelain
crafts.look: Glazed white bone china with blue painted flowers and birds, fired in a regimental kiln; every old crack mended in gold, so the limbs are veined with gold lines.
crafts.hit: A sharp ceramic clack with a bell-like china ring and a tinkle of chips.
crafts.breaks: Shatters into blade-sharp shards that cut both fighters.
crafts.bleeds: Porcelain does not bleed; the shards it sheds make the other fighter bleed instead.

cue.prompt: A hard porcelain hand strikes flesh: a sharp ceramic clack with a bright china ring and a little tinkle of chips falling. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Ship's Oak
crafts.look: Weathered grey-brown oak from a warship's timbers, iron-banded at the joints, the seams caulked with black tar, barnacles on the elbows and knees.
crafts.hit: A deep wooden knock and a creak, like a mallet driven into a ship's timber.
crafts.breaks: Splinters into long stakes and spits tar.
crafts.bleeds: Splinters and tar with the blood; the splinters stay in the other fighter.

cue.note: an oak elbow driving into a body
cue.prompt: A heavy oak elbow drives into a body: a deep wooden knock with a short timber creak after it. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Aether Glass
crafts.look: Blown-glass tubes and bulbs in brass ferrules, filled with a glowing coloured gas that brightens with every move, like a lit sign in the rain.
crafts.hit: A bright glass clink over a low electric buzz, with a soft whump of gas.
crafts.breaks: Shatters and spits burning gas; it refills from a reservoir in the hip a second later.
crafts.bleeds: Burning gas and glass with the blood; wounds glow for a moment.

cue.note: a glowing glass shin kicking into a body
cue.prompt: A glass shin full of glowing gas kicks into a body: a bright glass clink over a low electric buzz and a soft whump of gas. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Foundry Iron
crafts.look: Black sand-cast iron with rough seams, rivets the size of thumbs, and grated vents that glow orange from the coals inside.
crafts.hit: A deep iron gong-thud with a hiss of steam.
crafts.breaks: Cracks and spills glowing coals across the floor, where they hiss in the water.
crafts.bleeds: Iron does not bleed; it cauterises, so wounds it makes smoke.

cue.note: a cast-iron fist crushing into a body
cue.prompt: A huge cast-iron fist crushes into a body: a deep dull iron thud with a low ringing and a short hiss of steam. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Jet and Whalebone
crafts.look: Polished black mourning jet in faceted beads and plates over cream whalebone stays, laced like a corset with black silk ribbon; the joints bend further than a joint should.
crafts.hit: A creak of lacing pulled tight, a click of jet beads and a soft snap.
crafts.breaks: The lacing parts and the stays spring loose in a fan.
crafts.bleeds: Little blood of its own; the stays take blood into the lacing, which goes from black to darker.

cue.note: a jet and whalebone arm wrapping and snapping on a body
cue.prompt: A stiff corseted arm snaps tight round a body: a creak of lacing pulled hard, a click of glass beads and a soft bony snap. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Silver and Ebony
crafts.look: Black ebony limbs sheathed in hallmarked silver filigree, fluted like a candlestick, the family crest engraved at the shoulder; polished to a mirror between bouts.
crafts.hit: A clean bright ring like a struck silver tray over a hard ebony clack.
crafts.breaks: The silver bends and the ebony splits along the grain.
crafts.bleeds: Silver never bleeds. Blood beads on it and runs off, and he polishes it away.

cue.note: a silver and ebony hand cutting into flesh
cue.prompt: A silver-sheathed ebony hand cuts into flesh: a clean bright ring like a struck silver tray over a hard wooden clack and a short wet slice. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Grafted Bear
crafts.look: A bear's forelimbs and hind legs sewn on at the shoulder and hip with surgical gut and brass staples; matted brown fur, black claws, the stitching weeping.
crafts.hit: A heavy meaty thump with fur in it and a low animal grunt.
crafts.breaks: The stitching tears and the limb hangs by a flap; it bleeds more than anything else in the Sump.
crafts.bleeds: Thick dark blood soaks the fur and drips from it for the rest of the match.

cue.note: a furred bear paw clubbing a body
cue.prompt: A huge furred paw clubs a body: a heavy meaty thump with a rough brush of fur and a low animal grunt. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

crafts.name: Pawnshop Patchwork
crafts.look: Whatever was in the pawnbroker's window: a mismatched set from the other eleven crafts, each limb with a paper pawn ticket tied on with string, numbered.
crafts.hit: Each limb sounds like its own craft, so every hit sounds different.
crafts.breaks: As its own craft; the pawn ticket flutters off.
crafts.note: The limbs are rolled from the other crafts at the start of each bout. The game already rolls a limb's traits per match (src/sim/limbs.ts); this is the same idea, made visible.

crafts.name: Bamboo and Samovar
crafts.look: Lacquered amber bamboo canes bound in engraved brass hoops, miniature pressurized tea boilers, turn-taps at the wrists hissing white jasmine steam.
crafts.hit: A hollow wooden clack with a bright brass ting and a sharp hiss of steam.
crafts.breaks: Bamboo splinters along the grain and boiling water sprays from the samovar valves.
crafts.bleeds: Amber fermented tea and steam mix with the blood.

cue.prompt: A hollow bamboo cane strikes flesh: a woody clack with a bright brass ting and a short hiss of steam. Close microphone, dry room, one single impact.

characters.name: Constable Obadiah Winch
characters.blurb: Twenty-two years on the beat and three clockwork limbs. He will caution you first.
characters.title: The Wound Constable

profile.from: Lamplight Row Station, C Division of the Watch, the Drench
profile.bio: Obadiah Winch walked the same beat along the drowned end of Lamplight Row for twenty-two years and was never once late. In the Cab Riot of the ninetieth year of the rain he held the Row alone for six hours and lost both arms and his left leg under the wheels. The Watch Benevolent Fund bought him new ones from a clockmaker on Crutch Street: brass regulator movements, wound by a key between his shoulder blades. The Fund does not pay for the winding oil. So on his nights off he puts on his helmet, signs in at the Sump, and fights for the price of oil and the widows of C Division. He arrests every opponent he beats. Nobody has ever told him that the Sump is outside the law, and nobody will.
profile.personality: Patient, plain, immovable. He believes in the beat, the rota and the notebook. He has never hit a man without cautioning him first, and he never stops hitting a man until the caution is complete.
profile.manners: Addresses everyone by rank or as 'sir' and 'madam'. Touches his helmet to the Gallery. Cautions every opponent before the bell. Writes down the name of everyone he beats and the time.
profile.violence: His brass limbs feel nothing, so he cannot tell when he has broken something and keeps going until the clockwork runs down. He handcuffs wrists to ankles and leaves people folded in the rain.
profile.otherSelf: Overwound: the key turned past the stop. The ticking becomes a scream, the caution becomes a roar, and the Constable becomes the riot he once stood against.

rivals.why: He has arrested her eleven times. She has escaped eleven times, once through a drain he was standing on.

partner.why: She rebuilt his first leg in a field ward. He walks her home after every bout.

quotes.intro: Evening, all. Anything you say will be taken down. So will you.
quotes.appeal: Ladies and gentlemen of the Gallery: is this not the very picture of public order?
quotes.victory: Nothing to see here. Move along, please. Mind the blood, madam.
quotes.defeat: Tell the Fund... I was on my beat.

limbs.arms: Both arms, shoulder to fingertip: brass regulator housings with glass windows over the escapement, each finger on its own little spring.
limbs.legs: The left leg from mid-thigh, with a rolled trouser leg so the Gallery can see the pendulum swing in the shin. The right leg is still his own.
limbs.wear: Dents show where he was hit. When the mainspring runs low his strikes slow down and the ticking drops a tone; a big hit can stop an arm dead until he slaps it.

profile.from: Smelt & Sons Ironworks, the Furnace Quarter
profile.bio: Hezekiah Smelt has cast every railing, bridge and lamp post in Old Sorrow, and he owns the foundry that cast them. There are no sons; Smelt & Sons was named for the four great furnaces, which he loves. When the fumes took his lungs his own pattern-makers cast him a new body: a cast-iron frame round a coal boiler where his chest was, iron arms like bridge girders, and a chimney that rises through the crown of his stovepipe hat. He endows orphanages, where the children work only fourteen hours, and he fights in the Sump because the Society's charter makes the winner its chairman. He has been chairman for nine years.
profile.personality: Expansive, generous with his money, entirely without mercy. Everything is an investment. He is pleased to see you, and he is pleased to see you broken.
profile.manners: Shakes every hand, gently, which is the only gentle thing he does. Thanks the Gallery for their patronage and refers to his opponents as 'my dear sir' and 'my dear madam'.
profile.violence: Slow, inevitable, crushing. He picks people up and presses until something gives. Molten slag pours from the vents in his palms.
profile.otherSelf: Stoked: he drinks a draught of coal oil, the boiler roars, the chimney spits flame and his iron glows red. He stops speaking and just breathes.

rivals.why: Smelt's ironclads put the wooden navy out of service. He bought Rook's ship for scrap and burned her in his furnace.

characters.blurb: A chapel-going mudlark with drainpipe arms full of rainwater. She says grace before she bites.
characters.title: The Mudlark

profile.from: the mud under Lament Bridge, the Drench
profile.bio: Nell Sluice was born on the mud under Lament Bridge and has picked it for coins, rings and teeth since she could walk. At twelve the Lament sluice gates closed on her arms. A plumber from the Bethel Chapel soldered her new ones out of the lead drainpipe that had carried the flood: hollow, heavy, open at the shoulder to the rain. They fill as she fights, and full they hit like a bridge pier. She teaches Sunday school, sings in the choir, and sends every penny from the Sump to the Chapel's Fund for Drowned Children. She has never once been caught stealing, by anyone but Constable Winch.
profile.personality: Cheerful, devout, relentless. A force of nature in a shawl. She forgives everyone for everything as she is doing it.
profile.manners: Says grace before every bout. Calls everyone 'pet' and 'my love'. Thanks the opponent for every blow they land on her. Crosses herself over the fallen.
profile.violence: Rushes in like floodwater and does not stop. Drowns people in the puddles of the Sump. Bites.
profile.otherSelf: Flood Tide: she drinks a bottle of river water from under the bridge and the arms fill until the solder weeps. She stops forgiving.

rivals.why: Eleven arrests, eleven escapes. She thinks of him fondly.

partner.why: Her lodger. She feeds him and pawns his things to pay his rent.

profile.from: the Royal Sorrow Infirmary, the Heights; formerly the field wards of the Sorrow Wars
profile.bio: Prudence Kilnworth ran the field wards through four years of the Sorrow Wars and lost her arms and her right leg to a shell that landed on the operating tent. The regiment's kiln, which fired its mess china, fired her new ones: white bone porcelain painted with blue flowers, jointed with silver pins. Every crack she has taken since has been mended in gold, and there are a great many. She runs the Infirmary like a barracks, and she fights in the Sump because the Infirmary has no money and because she has seen how a body comes apart and is professionally interested in doing it properly. A clean break heals better, she says. She breaks very cleanly.
profile.personality: Brisk, exact, incorruptible, terrifying. She has no patience for weakness and endless patience for procedure.
profile.manners: The bedside manner: 'Now then.' 'This won't hurt a bit.' 'Chin up.' Corrects her opponent's posture, and her own. Thanks the Gallery for their contributions.
profile.violence: Surgical: she finds the joint and breaks it, names the bone as she does, and moves to the next. Her strikes are short, exact, drilled.
profile.otherSelf: Lights Out on the Ward: the night-nurse's draught. The gold in her cracks glows white-hot and the porcelain sings, and she stops naming the bones.

rivals.why: A drunk who calls his rum medicinal. She treated his scalds once, and he poured her a cup of it.

partner.why: She fitted his first leg in a field ward. He brings her flowers.

profile.from: the Alhambra of Varieties, Gaiety Lane
profile.trade: Strongman, wrestler, champion of the Halls
profile.bio: For fifteen years the Great Bartholomew Mule wrestled Old Ursula, a dancing bear, twice nightly at the Alhambra of Varieties, and never once lost. When Old Ursula died he could not bear to part with her. A surgeon on Crutch Street sewed her forelimbs onto his shoulders and her hind legs onto his hips, and an apothecary sells him the ursine tincture that keeps the graft from rotting. The act has never been better. He wears the Diamond Belt of the Halls, which he won from himself, and fights in the Sump because the music halls are dying and the Sump is the last great stage in Old Sorrow.
profile.personality: Grandiloquent, sentimental, vain, enormous. Every bout is a performance and every opponent a valued member of the company.
profile.manners: The showman's courtesy. Introduces his opponent to the Gallery with a flourish, bows to them, and kisses the hands of the ladies in the front row. Thanks everyone. Weeps at the end.
profile.violence: He wraps them up and crushes them: bear hugs that burst ribs, claws that open faces, and bites. The bear in him wants to eat.
profile.otherSelf: The Bear Within: a double dose of the ursine tincture. His fur grows over his face, he drops to all fours between moves, and he roars instead of speaking.

rivals.why: She called his act vulgar in the papers. He has her cutting framed in his dressing room.
The undertaker had already bought Old Ursula's body. Mule had the arms off her before Crape's cart arrived.

partner.why: Mule brings in heavy scrap iron lasts and railway boots; Tabitha welds them into indestructible weapons and braces for him.

profile.from: the hulks moored off Grief Reach
profile.trade: Bosun of the late warship Indefatigable Grief
profile.bio: Absalom Rook was bosun of the wooden warship Indefatigable Grief for thirty years and learned the art of eight limbs from boxers in a dozen far ports. When the iron navy came, the Grief was sold for scrap to Smelt & Sons and broken up in their yard. Rook bought back her knees, the curved oak braces that held her decks to her hull, and had them fitted as his own knees and elbows, iron-banded and caulked with her tar. He lives on a prison hulk off Grief Reach with the last of her crew, and fights in the Sump to buy back the rest of her, one timber at a time.
profile.personality: Gruff, loyal, superstitious, deeply mournful. He keeps the old naval forms because they are all that is left.
profile.manners: Asks permission to come aboard before every bout and pipes the side for his opponent on his bosun's call. Calls every opponent 'sir', even when he is breaking their neck. Says a prayer for the drowned at the end.
profile.violence: Elbows like mallets, knees like rams, a clinch like a ship's cable. He drags people round like a sail being taken in.
profile.otherSelf: All Hands: a double tot of the bosun's rum. The oak swells and creaks, he stops feeling anything, and he sings sea shanties while he kills.

profile.bio: Lady Hester Bulwark boxed in secret at her finishing school and was expelled for breaking the dancing master's jaw. When her father the Earl lost Bulwark Hall at cards, he took to his rooms and his tonics, and Hester took his steam yacht to the breakers and had its steering rams fitted to her own forearms: blued steel pistons that fire on every punch, fed by a little boiler in her bustle. She boxes under the Marchioness's rules, which she wrote, and means to win back the Hall in the Sump before her engagement to Sir Peregrine Ashby-Lisle can be announced. She would rather kill him than marry him. She may do both.
profile.personality: Cool, crisp, competitive, quietly furious. Every bout is a matter of family honour and she will not lose it.
profile.manners: Perfect: a curtsey, a handshake with the glove off, 'Do forgive me,' 'How very kind.' Never raises her voice. Apologises for the steam.
profile.violence: Precision boxing with a ram behind every punch. Her jabs go through faces. When the pistons fire at full stroke, things burst.
profile.otherSelf: The Family Tonic: her father's madness in a silver flask. The pressure goes into the red, the gauges crack, and she stops being a lady about it.

rivals.why: She called his act vulgar in the Morning Lamp. He has been trying to hug her ever since.
The Bulwark gas company attempted to seize Pegg's Spitalfields workshop for a coal storage depot; Tabitha drove Hester's bailiffs into the street with a flurry of iron shoe lasts.

profile.bio: Percival Crump spent thirty years along the Pearl River tea factories before a dock crane collapsed his arms. Rather than accept wooden pegs, he commissioned lacquered bamboo prosthetics housing miniature brass samovar boilers that brew scalding fermented tea. In combat, he appears hopelessly tipsy, swaying with daintily balanced porcelain teacups, only to unleash devastating Drunken Kung Fu with clouds of scalding jasmine steam.

profile.manners: Apologizes profusely for spilling scalding tea on opponents; insists on offering a fresh cup before snapping a collarbone.
profile.violence: Fluid, unpredictable, swaying strikes with bamboo elbows and palm heel thrusts accompanied by hissing steam vents.
profile.otherSelf: Over-Steeped: he downs a flask of 100-proof fermented pu-erh rum; the samovar vents shriek like teakettles, and his swaying becomes lightning-fast.

profile.bio: Tabitha Pegg spent fourteen years hammering box calf and pigskin over iron lasts in the damp cellars of Spitalfields, until an industrial steam-press crushed both her feet during a rush order for the Royal Horse Guards. Rather than beg, Pegg shut herself in her workshop for six months and emerged on legs of her own forging: articulated cast-iron shoemaker lasts, calibrated brass measuring calipers, and heavy triple-soled steel brogues fitted with spring-ratchet clockwork. She treats human combat as an exacting sizing problem—every knee strike, roundhouse, and spinning hook kick measured to the millimeter and driven home with thirty pounds of cold pig-iron.
profile.personality: Methodical, acerbic, relentlessly exacting. She views every opponent not as a fighter, but as an ill-fitting boot that needs stretching, paring down, or hammering flat.
profile.manners: Takes chalk from behind her ear and marks the opponent's lapel or cheek before kicking it. Measures distances with a brass sliding gauge. 'Stand straight; you're throwing my welt off.'
profile.violence: Rapid-fire machine-gun kicks with mathematical precision. High-speed staccato Tae Kwon Do roundhouses, piercing steel-tipped toe jabs, and shattering iron-welt heel drops.
profile.otherSelf: Overwound Springs: she clicks a tension ratchet behind her knee; the clockwork springs scream at double speed, unleashing an uncontrollable blizzard of rhythmic kicks.

rivals.why: Smelt's chimney-sweep furnace soot ruins her fine top-grain box calf leather and gums up her knee ratchets.
The Bulwark gas company attempted to seize Pegg's Spitalfields workshop for a coal storage depot; Tabitha drove Hester's bailiffs into the street with a flurry of iron shoe lasts.

partner.why: Mule brings in heavy scrap iron lasts and railway boots; Tabitha welds them into indestructible weapons and braces for him.

profile.bio: Crape & Daughter have buried Old Sorrow's dead for four generations. The present Mr. Crape lost the use of his arms and legs to a wasting illness in his youth, and his daughter, who was the joiner of the firm, made him new ones from the stock: mourning jet over whalebone stays, laced like a widow's corset, jointed so they bend any way a body needs to be bent. His daughter has since died, and is on display in the shop window, very nicely done. He takes every opponent's measurements before the bell and has a coffin built to them. If they do not fit it at the end of the bout, he makes them fit. He fights in the Sump because it is very good for business.
profile.personality: Solemn, gentle, soft-spoken, unhurried. He is comforting. He is the last face many people see and he takes that seriously.
profile.manners: Condolences: 'My deepest sympathies,' 'We'll have you looking your best.' Removes his hat. Takes measurements with a tape. Never touches anyone roughly, even while folding them in half.
profile.violence: Submissions and dislocations: he folds people. Arms behind backs, knees past ears, spines into boxes. Judo throws into the floor followed by a lock that finishes it.
profile.otherSelf: The Last Measure: a draught of embalming fluid. His face goes grey, his lacing tightens, and his holds cannot be broken.

characters.name: Sir Peregrine Ashby-Lisle, Bt.
characters.blurb: Forty-one duels, silver arms, a swordstick and impeccable manners. He is so terribly sorry.
characters.title: The Most Courteous Man in Old Sorrow

profile.from: Lisle House, Regent's Terrace, the Heights
profile.trade: Baronet, duellist, patron of the arts
profile.bio: Sir Peregrine Ashby-Lisle has fought forty-one duels and apologised before, during and after every one. He lost his right arm in the ninth and his left in the twenty-sixth, and the family silversmiths made him new ones: ebony sheathed in hallmarked silver filigree, with the Ashby-Lisle crest at each shoulder. He carries a swordstick and, for emergencies, a little pepperbox pistol, and he is the finest blade in Old Sorrow. He sends flowers and a handwritten card of condolence to every widow he makes, and he has made a great many. He fights in the Sump because a gentleman must have an occupation, because he is very deeply in debt, and because he is engaged to Lady Hester Bulwark, who intends to kill him, and he would like to be in practice.
profile.personality: Charming, gentle, considerate, utterly and serenely monstrous. He is incapable of rudeness and incapable of mercy, and sees no contradiction.
profile.manners: The most courteous man in the city. Bows, removes his hat, asks permission ('Might I trouble you for your spine?'), apologises with every cut, thanks his opponents warmly, and never once raises his voice. He tips the Sump's attendants. He remembers everyone's name. He writes the condolence card during the bout.
profile.violence: Horrific. He flays, he carves, he disembowels with the swordstick in long, neat, unhurried strokes, and he carves his monogram into his opponents as a courtesy, so the family knows who to write to.
profile.otherSelf: The Other Sir Peregrine: a drop of the family tonic in his tea. He is still perfectly polite, but now the apologies are screamed, the silver tarnishes black, and he laughs.

rivals.why: Inkle is the junior clerk at the firm that holds the Ashby-Lisle debts, and keeps serving him notice. Sir Peregrine is very fond of him and intends to kill him gently.

partner.why: His intended. They waltz beautifully, and he admires her very much.

characters.name: Mr. Cuthbert Inkle
characters.blurb: He pawned his own arms and legs and fights in borrowed ones. Terribly sorry, he's never done this before.
characters.title: The Articled Clerk

profile.from: a back room at Nell Sluice's, Lament Court
profile.trade: Articled clerk at Pinchbeck & Gall, Solicitors
profile.bio: Cuthbert Inkle copies deeds at Pinchbeck & Gall for seven shillings a week. To keep his widowed mother out of the Marshalsea he pawned his own arms and legs one at a time at Uncle Gideon's on Crutch Street, and then, being unable to work without arms, rented them back by the week. He cannot afford his own. On bout nights he borrows whatever is in Uncle Gideon's window that evening, each limb with its pawn ticket still tied on: a porcelain arm, a glass leg, a bear's paw, whatever has come in. He has never been in a fight and does not know how. Once he starts, he cannot stop, and he is horrified by himself every time.
profile.personality: Timid, earnest, kind, desperate. A small man in a very big trouble, who turns out to be capable of absolutely anything.
profile.manners: Abject. Apologises to his opponent, the Gallery, the referee and the furniture. Calls everyone 'sir', including the ladies, and then apologises for that. Tries to shake hands at the wrong moments.
profile.violence: Panic-violence: wild, flailing, unskilled, and it does not stop once it starts. He stabs with the steel nib of his pen. The borrowed limbs do things he did not ask them to.
profile.otherSelf: In Arrears: a swig of gin for courage. Every limb he has on is swapped at random for another from the pawnshop, and something in his face goes very still.

rivals.why: He has served Sir Peregrine notice of debt nine times. Sir Peregrine always thanks him beautifully and has promised to kill him gently.

partner.why: His landlady. She feeds him, prays for him, and pawns his things for the rent.
